objectives.en: Describe the latitudinal gradient in diversity and its explanations
Use the species–area relationship S = CA^Z

narration.en: Colombia, near the equator, has about 1,400 species of birds. Greenland, far to the north, has 56. Biodiversity follows clear patterns across the globe and with area.
narration.kn: ಸಮಭಾಜಕದ ಬಳಿಯ ಕೊಲಂಬಿಯಾದಲ್ಲಿ ಸುಮಾರು 1,400 ಪಕ್ಷಿ ಪ್ರಭೇದಗಳಿವೆ. ಉತ್ತರದ ಗ್ರೀನ್‌ಲ್ಯಾಂಡ್‌ನಲ್ಲಿ 56. ಜೀವವೈವಿಧ್ಯ ಭೂಗೋಳದಾದ್ಯಂತ ಮತ್ತು ವಿಸ್ತೀರ್ಣದೊಂದಿಗೆ ಸ್ಪಷ್ಟ ಮಾದರಿ ಅನುಸರಿಸುತ್ತದೆ.

body.en: In general, species diversity decreases as we move away from the equator towards the poles. With very few exceptions, tropics (latitudinal range 23.5° N to 23.5° S) harbour more species than temperate or polar areas. Colombia, near the equator, has nearly 1,400 species of birds, while New York at 41° N has 105 species and Greenland at 71° N only 56 species. India, with much of its land area in the tropics, has more than 1,200 species of birds. A forest in a tropical region like Ecuador has up to 10 times as many species of vascular plants as a forest of equal area in a temperate region like the Midwest of the USA. The largely tropical Amazonian rain forest in South America has the greatest biodiversity on Earth: more than 40,000 species of plants, 3,000 of fishes, 1,300 of birds, 427 of mammals, 427 of amphibians, 378 of reptiles and more than 1,25,000 invertebrates. Ecologists explain this by: (a) speciation is generally a function of time; temperate regions were subjected to frequent glaciations in the past, while tropical latitudes remained relatively undisturbed for millions of years and so had a long evolutionary time for species diversification; (b) tropical environments, unlike temperate ones, are less seasonal, relatively more constant and predictable, which promotes niche specialisation and leads to greater species diversity; (c) there is more solar energy available in the tropics, which contributes to higher productivity, which in turn might contribute indirectly to greater diversity.

points.en: Diversity decreases from the equator to the poles
Birds: Colombia ~1,400; New York (41° N) 105; Greenland (71° N) 56; India >1,200
Reasons: long undisturbed time, constant environment, more solar energy

narration.en: Species diversity decreases from the equator to the poles: Colombia has about 1,400 bird species, Greenland only 56. The tropics had a long undisturbed time for speciation, have a more constant environment that allows niche specialisation, and receive more solar energy.

They have stayed undisturbed for millions of years, their climate is less seasonal and more constant, and they get more solar energy. Humboldt noticed that species richness rises with the area explored, but more and more slowly: a rectangular hyperbola. On a log scale it becomes a straight line whose slope is Z. Humboldt saw that more area holds more species, but only up to a point. Move the area and watch the species count. Then switch to log–log axes: the curve straightens into a line whose slope is Z.

caption.en: Species richness S rises with area A but more and more slowly: S = C × A^Z. On ordinary axes this is a curve; on log–log axes it is a straight line of slope Z. Z is about 0.1–0.2 for most regions, but 0.6–1.2 for very large areas such as whole continents.
caption.kn: ವಿಸ್ತೀರ್ಣ ಹೆಚ್ಚಿದಂತೆ ಪ್ರಭೇದ ಸಮೃದ್ಧಿ ಹೆಚ್ಚುತ್ತದೆ ಆದರೆ ನಿಧಾನವಾಗಿ: S = C × A^Z. ಲಾಗ್–ಲಾಗ್ ಅಕ್ಷಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಇದು Z ಇಳಿಜಾರಿನ ನೇರ ರೇಖೆ. ಹೆಚ್ಚಿನ ಪ್ರದೇಶಗಳಿಗೆ Z ಸುಮಾರು 0.1–0.2; ಖಂಡಗಳಂತಹ ದೊಡ್ಡ ಪ್ರದೇಶಗಳಿಗೆ 0.6–1.2.

body.en: During his pioneering and extensive explorations in the wilderness of South American jungles, the German naturalist and geographer Alexander von Humboldt observed that within a region, species richness increased with increasing explored area, but only up to a limit. The relation between species richness and area for a wide variety of taxa (angiosperm plants, birds, bats, freshwater fishes) turns out to be a rectangular hyperbola; on a logarithmic scale it is a straight line, described by log S = log C + Z log A, where S = species richness, A = area, Z = slope of the line (regression coefficient) and C = Y-intercept. Ecologists have found that the value of Z lies in the range 0.1 to 0.2, regardless of the taxonomic group or the region. But for very large areas like entire continents, the slope is much steeper, with Z values in the range 0.6 to 1.2. For example, for frugivorous (fruit-eating) birds and mammals in the tropical forests of different continents, the slope is 1.15.

points.en: Rectangular hyperbola; straight line on log scale
Z = 0.1–0.2 for most regions and taxa
Whole continents: Z = 0.6–1.2; frugivorous birds and mammals: 1.15

narration.en: Humboldt found that species richness rises with area, but only up to a limit. On a log scale, log S equals log C plus Z log A; Z is usually 0.1 to 0.2, but for whole continents it is much steeper, 0.6 to 1.2.
narration.kn: ವಿಸ್ತೀರ್ಣ ಹೆಚ್ಚಿದಂತೆ ಪ್ರಭೇದ ಸಮೃದ್ಧಿ ಒಂದು ಮಿತಿಯವರೆಗೆ ಹೆಚ್ಚುತ್ತದೆ ಎಂದು ಹಂಬೋಲ್ಟ್ ಕಂಡರು. ಲಾಗ್ ಮಾಪನದಲ್ಲಿ log S = log C + Z log A; Z ಸಾಮಾನ್ಯವಾಗಿ 0.1 ರಿಂದ 0.2, ಆದರೆ ಇಡೀ ಖಂಡಗಳಿಗೆ 0.6 ರಿಂದ 1.2.
